analysis.one_liner: Makes home and community-based care a required Medicaid benefit, with the federal government paying the full cost.
analysis.headline: Introduced August 6, 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill has had no hearing, markup, or vote; its 17 cosponsors are all Democrats or independents [S3][S4].
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make home and community-based services — help at home like personal care aides, home modifications, transportation, and respite for family caregivers — a mandatory Medicaid benefit in every state, rather than an optional program with waiting lists [S2]. It would raise eligibility so people with incomes up to roughly 150% of the poverty line could qualify, and it would have the federal government pay 100% of the cost of these services [S2]. It also funds grants to train, recruit, and retain the roughly 3.2 million low-paid direct care workers who deliver this care, and it would end Medicaid's practice of recovering costs from patients' estates after death [S2]. The new benefit would not take effect until five years after enactment [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities and older adults who need help with daily living but are stuck on state waiting lists or risk being placed in nursing homes; the roughly 63 million unpaid family caregivers, who would gain respite, support services, and the option of paid family caregiving; and the nearly 3.2 million direct care workers — mostly women, people of color, and immigrants — who would benefit from required reviews of pay rates and pass-through requirements that push rate increases to workers [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled people, older adults, and care workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every state Medicaid program to cover home and community-based services as a mandatory benefit, ending the waiver-by-waiver system that leaves hundreds of thousands on waiting lists [S2].
Sets the federal share of spending on these services at 100% for states that meet access and workforce conditions, so states cannot cite budget pressure to limit the service [S2].
Expands eligibility to people with incomes up to the greater of 150% of the poverty line or 300% of the SSI benefit rate, and lets states cover somewhat higher incomes at their option [S2].
Requires states to review and update payment rates at least every two years and to pass increases proportionately through to direct care workers, including in managed care contracts [S2].

Makes permanent protections against spousal impoverishment for people receiving home-based care, permanently extends the Money Follows the Person program that moves people out of institutions, and bars Medicaid from placing liens on or recovering costs from the estates of people who correctly received benefits [S2].

Appropriates $200 million for state quality metrics, $10 million for workforce recommendations, and $10 million for quality measurement, and funds grants for recruiting, training, and advancing direct care workers and for supporting family caregivers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended commitment to pay the entire cost of home and community-based services for a much larger eligible population; the bill contains no dedicated new revenue or offset, and states would cover a share of administrative costs [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill commits the federal government to paying 100% of the cost of a greatly expanded, open-ended benefit without any dedicated financing or offset to pay for it, which is the central objection any cost-focused lawmaker would raise [S2].

The mandatory benefit does not take effect until the first quarter beginning five years after enactment, so people on waiting lists today would see no relief for years even if the bill became law [S2].
Eligibility extends to households well above the poverty line — up to 150% of poverty or 300% of the SSI rate — which broadens who qualifies and adds to the federal cost [S2].

The bill allows states to impose provider taxes on home and community-based services to raise their share of funds, a financing device critics generally describe as shifting money in a circle between states, providers, and the federal treasury [S2].

States would face substantial new administrative duties — implementation plans, ombudsman offices, annual quality reporting, and two-year rate reviews — even with the higher federal match, and some states could struggle to build the workforce the bill assumes [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real and large: community care instead of institutionalization for disabled people and older adults, relief for family caregivers, and better pay for a workforce that today turns over at roughly 39% a year, a figure the bill's own findings cite [S2]. The serious cost is fiscal: an unlimited federal commitment to pay the full price of the expanded benefit with no financing attached, and a five-year delay before anyone gains access. Whether it is a good deal depends entirely on whether Congress is willing to fund it honestly, which this bill leaves to future budget fights.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it; with the Congress ending in early January 2027, it currently goes nowhere.

narrative.text: Senator Ben Ray Luján introduced the HCBS Access Act on August 6, 2026, with 15 Senate colleagues listed as original cosponsors [S2].
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since [S4].
The bill has 17 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents; no Republican has signed on [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, nothing has changed: the bill sits in committee, so states with waiting lists, the underpaid care workforce, and institutional care providers all keep the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; status quo holds

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Sanders, Warren, Baldwin, Duckworth, Fetterman, and Markey.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors are Democrats or independents, and no Republican has signed on; the referral to Finance, chaired by a Republican, has produced no action [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Home care and community-based service providers
industries.note: They would gain a much larger, mandatory customer base with full federal funding, and payment rates would be reviewed every two years with increases passed through to workers. More funding for their services directly expands care access for disabled and older people.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and other institutional care providers
industries.note: The bill would make it far easier for people to get care at home and would permanently fund the program that moves people out of institutions, reducing institutional census over time. Their business depends on the institutional settings the bill is designed to make avoidable.

They would administer a much larger benefit, but the bill requires that payment-rate increases be incorporated into managed care contracts rather than absorbed by the plans. Gains and costs both flow to them.

industries.industry: Labor unions representing direct care workers
industries.note: The bill gives union representatives seats on advisory panels, requires state infrastructure to cooperate with unions that represent these workers, and makes labor organizations eligible for workforce grants. Workers' wage interests and beneficiaries' access interests point the same way here.

States get 100% federal funding for the service itself and 80% for administration, but must take on implementation plans, quality reporting, ombudsman offices, and rate-setting duties. Most of the fiscal risk moves to Washington.

analysis.trajectory: With the 119th Congress ending January 3, 2027 and no committee action since the August 2026 referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or vote before the session ends; the usual path for a bill at this stage — no Republican cosponsors and no Finance Committee movement — is death at adjournment and reintroduction in the next Congress.
